name: Pale Salmon
lede: Pale Salmon is a light, pinkish orange, softer than the fish it is named after.

sections.title: Morganite, before the fire
sections.body:
The name is a lightened [[salmon]], the fish-flesh color [3]. It has few book mentions [3].

Finlay uses the words for a gem. A new pink beryl found on Madagascar in 1911 was named morganite, in thanks to the collector J. P. Morgan [1]. Freshly mined it tends to look a dull pale salmon, yet heat can turn it vivid, in Finlay's phrase like a bowl of raspberries [1]. The color of the raw stone is therefore not the color a jeweler sells [1]. Similar tones in our data include [[peach]] and [[apricot]] [3].

The swatch on this page is #FFB19A, the screen value we hold for it, which is an approximation and not a measured pigment [3]. Like any pale color it sits between its hue and [[white]], and because the name is a description and not a tradition, other lists may place it a little differently [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Pale Salmon appears in 20 of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, about 0.08 percent, as photographed [2]. The earliest dated one is from 1515, a work by Correggio, and the latest from 1923 [2].

questions.q: What color is raw morganite usually, per Finlay?
Morganite was named after a beryl discovery on Madagascar in 1911.

openers: Morganite comes out of the ground pale salmon and can look vivid after heating.
